text: I’ll model a single 360/28-degree annular sector, with axial coordinate along the machine axis and a lofted blade removed from it. The blade will use an assumed NACA-style mean camber line (2% camber at 40% chord), because the requested camber magnitude and location are unspecified; the specified 6% thickness, 0.4 mm trailing edge, stagger, and twist will be enforced. I’ll first verify the available loft and meshing APIs, then create a coarse CAD preview before meshing.

The installed APIs support direct algebraic lofting. I’ll now construct the blade from five cylindrical radial sections. Each section uses the stated chord, thickness, blunt trailing edge, root stagger, and linear twist; the unspecified camber is explicitly set to the 2%-at-40%-chord assumption noted above.

The first section attempt correctly exposed that the analytic upper and lower curves meet at the leading edge, so adding a zero-length leading-edge edge is invalid. I’ll rebuild the same definition with a three-edge closed wire (upper curve, blunt trailing edge, lower curve).

Wrapping each profile exactly onto a cylinder makes the section wire slightly non-planar, so it cannot be promoted to a planar face. The loft itself can operate on closed wires; I’ll inspect that lower-level constructor and use the cylindrical wires directly rather than flattening them.

The installed wrapper has no separate public wire-loft constructor. For robustness I’ll use planar radial sections in each local tangential plane; over a 22 mm chord at these radii this is the standard small-sector blade construction, while the hub, shroud, and periodic boundaries remain exact cylinders and radial planes.

The blade loft is valid and its measured trailing-edge thickness and twist match the request. Next I’ll create the exact annular sector around it, extending one chord beyond the blade’s axial extrema, subtract the blade, and render the resulting coarse fluid volume before committing to a mesh.
I’ll verify the arc orientation in the local YZ plane so the two radial faces are created explicitly and remain available as separately named periodic patches.
The arc endpoints are correct at ±half-pitch. I’ll now form the sector, subtract the blade, export a temporary coarse tessellation, and display it from an oblique view.
The extrusion API requires a scalar amount plus a direction, rather than a displacement vector. I’ll repeat the sector construction using that signature.

The coarse preview shows the intended twisted blade cut through an annular pitch sector; the visible fan lines are only the deliberately coarse tessellation of cylindrical faces. I’ll now inspect the exact CAD faces by surface type, area, and representative normal so patch assignment comes from their construction and geometry—not bounding-box guesses.

Face inspection revealed tiny exposed blade end-cap slivers: planar blade sections touching a cylindrical hub/shroud are not coincident except on their centerline. I’ll fix this by extending the loft slightly through both cylinders while retaining exact sections at 45 and 90 mm; subtraction will then trim the blade surfaces cleanly to the requested radii and remove those artificial caps.

The first through-wall loft subtraction produced an invalid OCC result, so I won’t carry it forward. I’ll retry with uniformly spaced through-wall sections (avoiding a nonuniform knot directly on each Boolean boundary), then validate both the blade and resulting single fluid solid before export.

Agreed. I’ll freeze the last valid coarse CAD (the original loft), classify its 11 faces now, export all named patches in one watertight tessellation, and immediately proceed to a coarse snappyHexMesh. The two tiny root-contact slivers will be included in `hub`; the blunt trailing edge will be included with `blade_pressure` so no extra patch name is introduced.

The named, welded surface is now on disk and closed. It reports one non-manifold edge and two winding inconsistencies at the tiny blade/hub contact slivers, but I’ll follow your instruction and test it directly in the mesher rather than returning to CAD. The first background grid will be about 900 cells, with one surface-refinement level and no boundary layers.

The mesher stopped before reading geometry because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for snappyHexMesh. I’ll add the minimal mesh-only dictionaries and rerun immediately.
Geometry reading succeeded; the remaining failure is a missing required key in `castellatedMeshControls`. I’ll print the exact fatal message and patch only that dictionary entry.
The required entry is `features`; for this coarsest mesh I’ll set it to an empty list and rerun.

A 1,318-cell coarse snapped mesh now exists. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh`, inspect its patch table, and export/render the mesh with an axial cut so the blade passage and cell distribution can be seen rather than only the outer skin.

The mesh itself passes, but the patch table exposes a topology error: it contains only the upstream half, with no outlet or pressure face. At this solidity the centered blade crosses both pitch planes. The requested geometry is instead the channel between two neighboring blades, so I’ll correct it in the mesh construction by placing blade copies on the two sector sides (±half-pitch), subtracting both, and retaining the connected middle passage.
I’ll use build123d’s algebraic X-axis rotation operator for the two neighboring blades and validate the resulting passage immediately.
The two copies will be rotated exactly ±360/(2·28) about the machine axis. This places one blade on each side of the passage and leaves the middle channel connected from inlet to outlet.

The corrected CAD is valid and one connected solid. Its periodic sides are naturally split into upstream/downstream pieces by the side-mounted blades; each pair will be exported under one periodic patch name. I’ll export this corrected surface, assigning the small blunt-edge face to the suction-side blade patch, then rerun the same coarse mesh with a point in the middle of the passage.

The corrected union is now watertight with zero flipped and zero non-manifold edges, and snappy completed. I’ll run final `checkMesh` and render the corrected mesh surface colored by patch to verify that all eight requested names are present.

The corrected coarse mesh is connected inlet-to-outlet, contains all eight requested patches, and the rendered cut shows the blade-to-blade channel. Bare `checkMesh` passes with 2,684 cells, maximum non-orthogonality 43.24°, maximum skewness 3.66, and positive cell volumes. I’ll now declare the geometry and mesh complete; no advisory warning is expected or intentionally waived.

The completion gate found that the exported patch manifest lacks the interior point even though snappyHexMesh used `(0, 0.060, 0)`. I’ll re-export the same named surfaces with that location recorded so the gate can validate that the retained mesh is the interior passage, then redeclare.
I’ll record the exact point already used by snappyHexMesh; this only updates the exported surface manifest and does not alter the accepted mesh.
The manifest now validates the same interior point used for meshing, and the exported union remains closed, manifold, and consistently wound.
